Now, I wish to go back to the first matter with which I was dealing and to say that in both the League of Nations and the International Labour organization Canada has the same status in the assembly and the conference as has every other member of these assemblies. Canada is also eligible for election to the council of the League and to the governing body of the international organization. In the labour organization Canada was actually elected a member of the governing body. The question of her status is not theory; it is a question of actual accomplished fact.	.
Our position and status in the League has been called in question by the reservations which have been adopted in the American Senate, and I think it is only right that I should bring the matter to the attention of the House, because it is a matter of vital concern to Canada. The reservation dealing with voting rights is generally known as the Lenroot Reservation. It is as follows:
The United States assumes no obligations to be bound by any election, decision, report, or finding of the Council or Assembly in which any member of the league and its self-governing dominions, colonies, or parts of the empire in the aggregate gives more than one vote, and

assumes no obligation to be bound by any decision, report, or finding of the Council or Assembly arising out of any dispute between the United States and any member of the League, if such member, or any self-governing Dominion, colony or part of empire united with it politically has voted.
Hon. members will see that this reservation contains two distinct proposals. First, the United States assumes no obligation to be bound by any election, decision or report in any dispute before the Council or Assembly in which any member of the League and its self-governing Dominions give more than one vote. The second part of the reservation deals with a dispute to which the United States is a party, and it states that it will not obligate itself to be bound in any such dispute if more than one vote is given by any member of the . League and any self-governing Dominions or Colonies politically united with it.
With the latter part of the reservation there is no ground of complaint, because it simply sets out what we understand to bo the effect and meaning of the Covenant as it stands. It is the first part of the reservation to which we cannot accede, because it challenges our whole position and status in the League. If the United States can claim that it is under no obligation to be bound by any decision in any dispute in which it is not a party, then all the other nations should be entitled to take the same position.
That reservation has since been somewhat modified, and as recently voted on in the Senate is in this form:
Until Part I, being the covenant of the League of Nations, shall be so amended as to provide that the United States shall be entitled-to cast a number of votes equal to that which any member of the League and its self-governing dominions, colonies, or parts of empire in the aggregate shall be entitled to cast, the-United States assumes no obligation to be bound, except in cases where Congress has previously given its consent, by any election, *decision, report, or finding of the Council or Assembly in which any member of the League and its self-governing dominions, colonies, or parts of empire in the aggregate have cast more than one vote.
In considering this reservation, Mr. Speaker, one must bear in mind the terms of the preamble, which, as originally drafted, was as follows:-
That the Senate advise and consent to the ratification of the Treaty of Peace with Germany concluded at Versailles on the 28th day of June, 1919, subject to the following reservations and understandings, which are hereby made a part, and condition of this resolution of ratification, which ratification is not to take effect or bind the United States until the said reservations and understandings adopted by

the Senate have been accepted by an exchange of notes as a part and a condition of this resolution of ratification by at least three of the four Principal Allied and Associated Powers, to wit, Great Britain, France, Italy and Japan.
Subsequently Mr. Lodge gave notice ol the following amended resolving clause:
That the Senate advise and consent to the ratification of the Treaty of Peace with Germany concluded at Versailles on the 28th day of June, 1919, subject to the following reservations and understandings, which are hereby made a part and condition of this resolution of ratification, which ratification is not to take effect or bind the United States until the said . reservations and understandings adopted by the Senate have been accepted as a part and a condition of this resolution of ratification by the Allied and Associated Powers, and a failure on the part of the Allied and Associated Powers to make objection to said reservations and understandings prior to the deposit of ratification by the United States shall be taken as a full and final acceptance of such reservations and understandings by said Powers.
The effect of this resolving clause is that none of the reservations that may be adopted by the United States Senate, can go. into effect unless they are accepted by all the Allied and Associated Powers. And they may be accepted by the Allied and Associated Powers by the failure of any one of these Powers to dissent within the time lflentioned in the resolving clause.
If, therefore, final action, should be taken in _ the form now proposed, the question which would face every nation party to the Covenant would be: Whether they would or would not assent to the reservations proposed by the United States. If they failed to dissent their assent would be presumed. It is on that account that Canada feels that there is only one possible course open to her, namely, that if any country should say that its ratification of the Treaty was conditioned upon our assenting to our own position being impaired, our status challenged, and our right to vote denied, we as a self-respecting people could not give that consent. Mr. Speaker, we all recognize the great importance of the United States coming into the League of Nations. No country is more interested in the United States coming in than Canada. We should be the last people in the world to put any obstacle in the way of her entry. I am sure that is the sentiment of. the country and of the House. But if the United States should finally say: " We will only come in on condition that you practically get out or have your status impaired," we can only reply: ".Well, you have a perfect right to say that if you choose, but we, as a self-respecting people, have an equal right to say ihat

we cannot accede to your terms." This position the Government has made perfectly clear to the proper authorities.
What is the constitutional position of Canada in relation to the other portions of the Empire at the present time? Some hon. members have said:	"You should not
change the constitution in any respect 'without first submitting the matter to Parliament." With a written constitution you could submit to Parliament any change which required legislative sanction. But the constitution of the British Empire is not embodied in any document. It is not a dead thing; it is a living thing. It grows from day to day and from year to year; it develops to meet exigencies and new conditions- as they aiise. That has been the history of the development of the British constitution. .

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
Is not our constitution
a written constitution?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
We are working under
the British North America Act, but that is not the whole constitution of the British Empire.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Have we any other?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
We have very important
rights outside the British North America Act, as I shall be glad to show my hon. friend. Up to time that the British North America Act was passed in 1867 and for many years thereafter, none of the Dominions were taken into consultation by the representatives of the Mother Country in matters of common Imperial concern. The first time they were called in consultation was in 1887, twenty years after Confederation, when the first Colonial Conference was held. That was not a formal gathering such as the Imperial Conference later became, but it was attended by representatives of the different self-governing colonies of the BritistPEmpire, as they were then called. It was the initiation of co-operation between what were then called the colonies and the Mother Country on an Empirewide scale. Because of its significaflce I wish to quote a few, words from the Marquis of Salisbury, then Prime Minister of Great Britain, on the occasion of the initiation pf this movement for co-operation and consultation throughout the Empire. He said:
We all feel the gravity and importance of this occasion. The decisions of this Conference may not he, for the moment, of vital importance; the business may seem prosaic, and may not issue in any great results at the moment. But we are all sensible that this meeting is the beginning of a state of things which is to have great results in the future. It will be the parent of a long progeniture, and distant councils of the Empire may, in some far-otf time, look back to the meeting in this room as the root from which all their greatness and all their beneficence sprang.
In that historic statement the Marquis of Salisbury saw into the future. He saw that the time' would come when there would be co-operation between the Mother Country and the Dominions along lines much more important, far-reaching and significant to the future of the Empire and of the world than that which was exemplified by the preliminary meeting held in 1887.
The next important step in the development of our constitutional relations was in 1897 when the first Conference, attended by the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was held. You will remember that in the session of the Canadian Parliament in 1897 the Government decided to grant the British Preference. That could not go into effect by reason of the existence of the Belgian and German treaties, and the matter was taken up during the sessions of the Imperial Conference in 1897. Speaking from recollection, I believe that a resolution was passed at that Conference urging the Mother Country to denounce those treaties. At that Conference it was agreed by the Mother Country that the treaties should he denounced, and they were denounced accordingly. When the Right Hon. Sir Wil-fiid Laurier returned to Canada after that meeting of the Colonial Conference he stated in very clear and very vigorous language what he conceived to be the result of that development. Speaking in Montreal, Toronto, and other parts of Canada,'he declared that by the action of the British Government in denouncing these treaties Canada had become a nation and that her name was known throughout Europe and the world. The Conference of 1897 marked a great advance over the Colonial Conference of 1887.
Ten years more elapsed,

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Do 1 understand the minister to say that as a result of these conferences and the fact that they a?e being held from time to time they have become part of our constitution? Suppose the British ceased to call these conferences* what would we do about it? What right have we to interfere?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
There is a difference between legal right and constitutional auth-

ority. There is nothing binding Great Britain to summon these conferences; we could not compel her to do so. But it has become the settled policy of the British Empire to summon these conferences; and the basis upon which they are now called is a resolution passed at the Conference of 1907, assented to by the Mother Country and all the Governments of the self-governing Dominions. It is quite true that the British Government could ignore this resolution, just as they could repeal the British North America Act. They have the legal right to do so, but they have no constitutional authority to do so, it would provoke a revolution if they exercised their legal right so far as the British North America Act is concerned. No man in the British Parliament would be insane enough to make such a suggestion.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Does the minister contend that Great Britain has not the constitutional authority not only to amend but even to repeal the British North America Act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: I said she had the legal right, but she has no constitutional authority to do so, because she has recognized now for nearly half a century the rights and privileges given us by the British North America Act.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
Does not the British
North America Act exist simply as a law of the British Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
The British Parliament
has in theory the legal right to impose taxation on Canada. That is, the constitution of the Empire has never been changed so as to take away from the Imperial Parliament, its legal right to legislate for the whole Empire. But they have no constitutional authority to legislate for Canada, they have no right to levy taxes on the self-governing Dominions. That is recognized by every statesman of the Empire; it is questioned by no one. No publicist, no man in Great Britain with any respect for his opinion, would venture to suggest that the British Parliament had any, such constitutional right.
Now, at the Colonial Conference of 1907, also attended by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, it was decided to change the name from " Colonial Conference " to " Imperial Conference " and to give it permanent form The following is the resolution:
That it will be to the advantage of the Empire if a conference, to be called the Imperial Conference, is held every four years, at which

questions of common interest may be discussed and considered as between His Majesty's Government and His Governments of the Self-governing Dominions beyond the seas.
The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom will be ex officio President, and the Prime Minister of the self-governing Dominions ex officio members, of the conference. The Secretary of State for the Colonies will be ex officio member of the conference and will take the chair in the absence of the president. He will arrange for such Imperial Conference after communication with the Prime Ministers of the respective Dominions.
Provision is made for a permanent secretariat, and that the conference shall meet once every five years. This resolution marked a great advance in the development of what one might describe as the constitution of the Empire. During the twenty year period from 1887 to 1907, the more or less casual meetings of the Colonial Conference for consultation had developed into a settled organization with fixed periods of meeting, and with certain defined subjects of common Imperial interest for consideration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman speaks of constitutional right. Would not the term "constitutional practice" be more appropriate?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
I am not concerned which term my hon. friend uses, because under the British constitution, constitutional practice develops into and becomes constitutional right, generates constitutional right. They become the conventions of the constitution and are just as binding, so far as the actual practice is concerned, as if we had a written constitution. It is because this constitutional practice can be developed into constitutional right, that the constitution of the Empire has proved itself so adaptable to meet all the changing needs and varying conditions which have surrounded the Empire in the course of its history.
In 1917, there was another and still more important constitutional development. In 1917 the Prime Minister of Great Britain called together the ministers of the' selfgoverning Dominions for consultation on vital matters of policy-relating to the prosecution of the war. They met as equals as Prime Ministers of the nations of the Empire! to discuss matters of common co'n-cern to the whole Empire. Great Britain recognized that with the growth in power and influence of the Dominions, the time had come when the Government of Great. Britain should frankly recognize that the Dominions had ceased to be in any sense States dependent upon the Mother Country,

and had become sister nations, standing on an equality with the Mother Country. It does not require, as I have already pointed out, any enactment of the Imperial Parliament to bring about that change; it has come about as a matter of constitutional practice. iBut certain constitutional adjustments will be necessary and provision was made for calling a constitutional conference in the future, as follows:
The Imperial War Conference are of opinion that the readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the Empire is too important and intricate a subject to be dealt with during the war, and that it should form the subject of a special Imperial Conference to be summoned as soon as possible after the cessation of hostilities.
They deem it their duty, however, to place on record their view that any such readjustment, while thoroughly preserving all existing powers of self-government and complete control of domestic affairs, should be based upon a full recognition of the Dominions as autonomous nations of an Imperial Commonwealth, and, of India as an important portion of the same, should recognize the right of the Dominions and India to an edequate voice in foreign policy and in foreign relations, and should provide effective arrangements for continuous consultation in all important matters of common Imperial concern, and for such necessary concerted action, founded on consultation, as the several Governments may determine.
I hold in my hand the report of the War Cabinet of the Government of Great Britain for the year 1918, and under the heading " Imperial Affairs -* on page 7, I find the following statement:
The common effort and sacrifice in the war have inevitably led to the recognition of an equality of status between the responsible Governments of the Empire. This equality has long been acknowledged in principle, and found its adequate expression in 1917 in the creation or rather the natural coming into being of an Imperial War Cabinet as an instrument for evolving a common Imperial policy in the conduct of the war. The nature of the constitutional development involved in the establishment as a permanent institution of the Imperial Cabinet system, was clearly explained by Sir Robert Borden in a speech to the Empire Parliamentary Association on the 21st of June, 1918.
The following is the ^extract from Sir Robert Borden's speech as set out in this official document of the British Government :
A very great step in the constitutional development of the Empire was taken last year by the Prime Minister when he summoned the Prime Ministers of the overseas Dominions to the Imperial War Cabinet. We meet there on terms of perfect equality. We meet there as Prime Ministers of self-governing nations. We meet there under the leadership and the presidency of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. After all, my Lord Chancellor and
Gentlemen, the British Empire, as it is at present constituted, is a very modern organization. It is perfectly true that it is built up on the development of centuries, but, as it is constituted to-day, both in territory and in organization, it is a relatively modern affair. Why, it is only 75 years since responsible government was granted to Canada. It is only little more than fifty years since the first experiment in Federal Government,-in a Federal Constitution,-was undertaken in this Empire. And from that we went on, in 1871, to representation in negotiating our Commercial Treaties, in 1878, to complete fiscal autonomy, and after that to complete fiscal control and the negotiation of our own treaties. But we have always lacked the full status of nationhood, because you exercised here a so-called trusteeship, under which you undertook to deal with foreign relations on our behalf, and sometimes without consulting us very much. Well, that day has gone by. We come here as we came last year, to deal with all these matters, upon terms of perfect equality with the Prime Minister of the Unitel Kingdom and his colleagues. It has been said that the term Imperial War Cabinet is a misnomer. The word 'Cabinet' is unknown to the law. The meaning of 'Cabinet' has developed from time to time.
I see no incongruity whatever in applying the term 'Cabinet' to the association of Prime Ministers and other ministers who meet around a common council board to debate and to determine the various needs of the Empire. If I should attempt to describe it, I should say it is a Cabinet of Governments. Every Prime Minister who sits around that board is responsible to his own parliament and to his own people; the conclusions of the War Cabinet can only be carried out by the parliaments of the different nations of our Imperial Commonwealth. Thus, each Dominion, each nation, retains its perfect autonomy. I venture to believe, and I thus expressed myself last year, that in this may be found the genesis of a development in the constitutional relation of the Empire, which will form the basis of its unity in the years to come.

And New Zealand?
Mr.	MACKENZIE	KING:	What	about
India?

And of the United Kingdom. India's position is not the same.

does it differ?	*
Mr.	ROWELL:	Because	India,	as a
nation, is not completely self-governing.
Mr.	MACKENZIE	KING:	What	about
Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Is not India given a place?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: India is given a place by the Peace Conference itself. Therefore, her status cannot be challenged; but it is by virtue of the place given her in the League by the Peace Conference that she acquires her rights.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Is it not correct that in the League of Nations Canada's status is not different from that of India?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Canada's status is not different from that of the other members of the League. Once they are members of the League by international recognition and consent, as embodied in the Treaty, they have the same rights.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: If I understand the minister correctly, he informs the House now that Canada's status as regards the League of Nations is identical with that of India.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: No, I did not say so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: But is not that true?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Once a nation is in the League, then under the terms of the League Covenant, it possesses all the - rights of membership; but if India had not been admitted by unanimous consent by delegates at the Peace Conference, she would not be entitled to admission under the terms of the Covenant and Canada would. If Canada had not been named in the Treaty Canada would be eligible for membership under the provision for admission of new States. India would not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: May I get this perfectly clear? At the present time has Canada in the League of Nations any rights or privileges which India has not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Surely I cannot make myself any clearer that every member cf the League of Natiops has the same rights.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: Then they have the same rights and privileges.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
India, by special agreement of all the nations, has been given the same right in the League as France, Great Britain, the United States, every other nation.
I presume that the reason why India has been given this exceptional treatment is because of the size of India-a nation of 300 millions-secondly, because of the part India took in the war, the magnificent contribution her troops made to the war, particularly in the East; thirdly, by reason of the fact that at that time there was before the Imperial House of Commons a proposal which has since become law under which India, in some important respects at least, obtains the right to manage her own affairs-the greatest experiment in the devolution of power from the Crown to the people which Great Britain has ever undertaken. By reason of these exceptional conditions a special case was made of India, and she was admitted as a member of the League; but, as I said, if she had not been admitted she would not have been qualified for membership under the terms and conditions on which new members can be admitted. Canada is qualified; Canada comes within the qualifications. If she had not been named in the Covenant, she would have been entitled to apply for admission, and should have been admitted. Therefore, their status is not the same.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: The minister has mentioned the Imperial War Cabinet. Is it his opinion that under our constitution there can be a cabinet without a Parliament to which that cabinet is responsible?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
As that point is discussed in the extract from the speech of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) I do not think it is necessary for me to take up the time of the House to deal with it now. My hon. friend will be able to read the extract in Hansard.
I have pointed out the status which the Dominions have under the treaty. I want also to point out that the position the Government of Canada has taken on this matter is fully supported by the Governments of the other Dominions. I have before me the debate in the South African Assembly on the Peace Treaty and the statement. of General Smuts. It is exactly to the same effect as the statement made by the Prime Minister and members of the Government to this House, namely, that the British Empire had become a commonwealth of nations, equal under a common sovereign. It is interesting to note that the objections made in the South African Parliament by Mr. Hertzog and his Nationalist associates were almost the same as those made in this Parliament, and the reply of General Urnuts to the criticism of the treaty is sub'-iantially

on the same lines as the reply of the Government to criticism of the treaty here. In view of the position of General Smuts as a great constitutional lawyer, and of the part he took in framing the Covenant of the League of Nations, and also as the Prime Minister of one of the other dominions of the Empire, I am sure hon. members would like to have his statement upon Hansard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext: The remarks I made a moment ago apply also to this document. It can only be put upon Hansard with the unanimous consent of the House.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
In moving the resolution to approve the treaty, General Smuts said:
The hon. gentleman who argued the previous motion last asked the question why there should be ratification by us, seeing that the British Parliament has already ratified this? He asked why we should trouble ourselves about this at all. Was it necessary for us, he asked, or was this merely a sham to putr before His Majesty the King. Hon. members by arguing that way only show that they do not know what the constitutional position is to-day. We have nothing to do with the ratification by the British Parliament. We signed this Treaty in Paris through the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence but His Majesty the King wishes the authority of the Union Parliament to ratify this. The King is not going to be influenced by the ratification given by the British House of Commons, and therefore the position is this, that until we have given the ratification which is necessary, until all the British Dominions who have signed this have agreed to this, ratification, we are, so far as the British Empire is concerned, hanging up this final exchange which is necessary before this Treaty is brought into force	
I remember when the report of our National Convention was made I made the statement that the most important thing about that document was the list of signatures at the end of it. And it is very much the same in regard to the Peace Treaty. For the first time in history the British Dominions signed a great international instrument, not only along with the other ministers of the King, but with the other ministers of the great powers of the world-(Hear, hear) -and although the tremendous importance of this great act has not yet been fully recognized there is no doubt that this Treaty, signed as it lias been with parties to it not only representative of the King in the British Isles, but in the Dominions, forms one of the most important landmarks in the history of the British Empire. .	.	. The British Dominions did not
fight for status. They went to war from a sense of duty, from their common interests with the rest of the world, vindicating the great principles of free human government. Not only has victory been achieved for the objects for which they fought, but, what for the British Dominions is equally precious, they have achieved international recognition of their status among the nations of the world. In a large sense this world is one of small nations, and certainly none of those had had larger results accruing to them from this war than the young nations of the British Empire. They have deserved this through the magnitude of their efforts. It has been proved and has never been challenged that
two of the British Dominions-Canada and Australia-made a greater war effort than any other powers below the rank of first-class powers. Their achievements have been outstanding ones. Australia alone lost more than the U.S.A. They have, of course, lost heavily; they are handicapped with enormous debt, but they have at any rate emerged with victory, honour, and a new standing in the world in that they are internationally recognized to-day. No wonder after what they have done that their great performance all through the war, and especially towards the end of it the other powers and nations of the world were only too willing to welcome and recognize them within the new great family. It took some time for the position to be realized at Paris, because so many of the powers were under the same impression which, according to the debate in the House that afternoon, appeared to exist in South Africa, viz., that everything seemed to be under tutelage of the British Parliament and Government. They could not realize the new situation arising, and that the British Empire, instead of being one central government, consisted of a league of free states, free, equal and working together for the great ideals of human government. It was difficult to make people realize this, but afterwards they fully applauded, and their approval was given as embodied in this international document. No doubt new forms would have to be made. No one recognized this more strongly than the British Government itself, but. whatever the forms, there was no doubt whatever about the substance of the new status of the Dominions.
There is the other aspect-the recognition which is thereby given to British Dominions in the League. The British Dominions are equal members, both in the Assembly and also with a. full right to be elected into the Council of the League. The Council consists of five great powers now, together with the representatives of four smaller powers, and among the latter which have to be elected on the Council of the League the British Dominions have the same right as any other power to be elected. I see in the American .Senate some difficulty has arisen about that, and they think that it is giving too large a vote to the British Empire. There is no doubt that there are British Dominions important enough in the near future to secure a seat on the Inner Council, and I can well understand that in other parts of the world this enormous preponderance which the British Empire will enjoy, and which may be accentuated, is not looked upon with very great favour. This matter of our status in the League of Nations was not one of the original conceptions of it. It took the British delegation at Paris a good deal of time to hammer out this new machinery for the recognition of young nations. The Dominions felt very strongly that here was their chance, and that if there was to be a League of Nations on which the nations were to be equally represented, then that League should include the British Dominions. We were determined to see that that recognition was given to us, but we were equally anxious to see that nothing was done which would loosen the ties which bind together the British Empire . (Cheers.) We kept both these things clearly before our eyes. iStill, we wanted our equality with the rest of the world recognized. We also wanted to remain in the British League of Nations, which has worked with such enormous success in the past-(cheers)-and has worked together in this war, probably becoming the real organizer of victory for all the Allies and the rest of the world. (Cheers.)

Fears have been expressed in, certain quarters, and fears have been given expressiion to in South Africa, that the ultimate tendency of the League of Nations would be to break up the British Empire, but that is an entirely misleading idea. On the contrary, I can well imagine great dominions arising which may be as important as Great Britain in the world, and if that motion had been dropped there would have been a danger of the breaking up of the British Empire. We have secured an inner League, and the world has agreed to it.
In his speech in reply on the resolution General Smuts stated:
As regards the question of status, General Smuts said that until last year British ministers had signed all documents and dealt with all matters affecting the Dominions. But a change had come about in Paris, when representatives of the Dominions had, on behalf of the King, for the first time signed that great document on behalf of the Dominions. The change was that in future the representatives of the Dominions would act for the Dominions. This precedent had now been laid down for the future. The British Constitution was most elastic, and the precedent might bring about the greatest changes. Where in the past British ministers could have acted for the Dominions, in future ministers of the Union would act for the Union. The change was a far-reaching one which would alter the whole basis of the British Empire. In future all parts of the British Empire stood on exactly the same basis. (General Hertzog: In the past you would have been put in prison for saying that.)
There was no misconception among British statesmen as to what the position was, and it was on that basis that matters had been agreed to in Paris	 The Dominions of the Empire would in future, therefore, stand on a basis of absolute equality. The British Empire would, therefore, be a league in which all the Dominions would be on an equal basis as regarded their Governments. The Prime Minister repeated that in the League of Nations, all the Dominions, with England, would stand on an equal footing, and would be recognized as such. The only difference would be that England would be a permanent member of the Central Council. Therefore, in future all parts of the Empire would equally be consulted in matters of war and peace:
I shall not take up the time of the House to quote Mr. Hughes or Mr. Massey, who took exactly the same position. Not only is that the position taken by the statesmen of the self-governing Dominions, but it is the position taken by the Government of Great Britain itself in reference to the effect of the Treaty of Peace. I have the statement of Lord Milner, Secretary of State for the Colonies made in an official statement issued by the Government of Great Britain, I shall be glad if it can be put upon Hansard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
I must again draw the attention of the House to the fact that it is most unusual to incorporate in Hansard any document that has not been read in the House, but in view of the importance of

this document, I take it that the House consents to its being incorporated in Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION AND SPEECH OF HON. N. W. ROWELL.
speechtext:
Lord Milner's statement
is as follows:
The Peace Treaty recently made in Paris was signed on behalf of the British Empire by ministers of the self-governing Dominions as well as by British ministers. They were all equally plenipotentiaries of His Majesty the King, who was the "High Contracting Party" for the whole Empire.
This procedure illustrates the new constitution of the Empire, which has been gradually growing up for many years past. The United Kingdom and the Dominions are partner nations ; not yet, indeed, of equal power, but for good and all of equal status. A time may come when one or more of these Dominions will equal or even surpass the United Kingdom in wealth and population, as they already surpass it in geographical extent. It is the paramount duty of British statesmanship to see to it that the free union between them and us, which has been so gloriously maintained during the war, shall be continued and strengthened in the years to come. If we are successful in that effort, the "Commonwealth of British Nations" will be the greatest instrument of peace and progress, the strongest influence making for freedom and civilization that the world has ever seen.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: During the war unity of policy between the self-governing states of the Empire was maintained by means of the "Imperial War Cabinet," and during the peace negotiations in Paris by the "British Empire delegation." In both these bodies Dominion ministers and British ministers sat and deliberated freely together, under the presidency of the British Prime Minister, and the policy of the Empire was thus shaped by consultation between. representatives of all its self-governing states.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
We have still to devise the means whereby this fruitful co-operation may be preserved in future, and the several independent nations of the Empire may always consult and act together on great international issues. The surest guarantee that such means will be found lies in a growing intimacy of intercourse between them. To foster that intimacy, to strengthen all the moral and material bonds which unite the different parts of the Empire, is a task to which we must constantly apply ourselves with the utmost energy. It is rendered easier by the progress of science, by inventions such as wireless telegraphy, the airship, and the aeroplane, which tend to annihilate distance. The encouragement of trade within the [DOT] Empire, of migration within the Empire, the progressive improvement of means of communication by sea and air, are the methods by which we must seek to strengthen that community of interest and of sentiment, which is the only sure foundation of Imperial unity.
I have quoted these statements to show that there is complete unanimity between the Government of Great Britain and the governments of the Dominions as to the

constitutional status of the different nations of the Empire. It is not a question of conflict of opinion or authority. All are agreed that the status is one of equality, that we are nations all equal in status, though not of equal power, under a common sovereign, and bound together by interest and sentiment, by ties which, though light as air, are strong as iron in binding together this League of Nations which we call the British Empire or the Britannic Commonwealth.
It goes without saying that there must be some constitutional readjustments in order to put into more practical and workable form the new situation that has developed, and it was in order that that might be done that provision was made in the year 1917 for the calling of a special Imperial Conference. When that conference is held-we do not know yet when it will be called-these questions must come up for consideration, and the representatives of Canada and the other dominions will attend, not as representatives of inferior or dependent nations, but as representatives of nations which by unanimous agreement are equal in status with the Mother Country. Canada's representatives will attend the conference, not for the purpose of creating any new Imperial organization, but for the purpose of developing a system of consultation and co-operation which will absolutely preserve the autonomy of the' dominions, and at the same time enable matters in which the dominions are vitally concerned to receive that attention and consideration by the dominions which, under the existing system, it is not possible to give them. I am sure all citizens of Canada desire to see this result secured.
What are the alternatives we must face if our position in the 'League could be Successfully challenged? We may go back into the old colonial position where the Mother Country would deal with all matters of foreign policy and settle for us the issues of peace and war, matters in which we are vitally interested. That, to my mind, is unthinkable. It is incredible that a young nation like Canada, with the achievements of this war to her credit and with the future opening before her, will ever consent to occupy a dependent position with reference to any country.
Then, Mr. Speaker, what is the other alternative? If we cannot stand on an equality within the Empire, the other alternative is Canadian independence. I say-and in this I voice the sentiment of the Government-that we stand unhesitatingly and unequivocally for the maintenance of the British connection.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why does my hon. friend limit that position to the Government? Why not say this Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I believe that is the position of this Parliament; I did not wish to convey any inference that any one differed. If we do not proceed along the line of equality of status and co-operation under a common sovereign, I submit that there are just two alternatives: Either dependency, with Great Britain controlling our foreign policy and the issues of peace or war, or independence, and we will not accept either alternative. If the reservation I have read, or anything similar in character, should be adopted finally by the Senate and approved by the President, and if it is stipulated as a condition of the ratification going into effect, that all the Allied Powers, parties to the Treaty, shall give their consent, and Canada gives her consent, she is relegated back into a colonial position and has not a voice and a vote among the nations of the world. That position is unthinkable; and we must, if we are to preserve our position and status and the unity of the British Empire, maintain our place in the family of nations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that any action of the United States could alter the status of this country in the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not unless we consent. If they submit as a condition of their ratification going into effect that we must consent, then the Government will not consent. In the exercise of our sovereign right to control our own affairs, we will not give our consent; hence the importance of Parliament standing behind the Government of Canada on this issue. Desiring, as we do, that there should be no misunderstanding, we thought the best way to avoid misunderstanding was to make our position clear, and this we have done to the proper authorities.

Suppose Great Britain
should accept these reservations, what would be our position?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not believe Great Britain would accept these reservations as against Canada's protest.

But supposing she did?
Mr, ROWELL: If Great Britain did and Panada dissented, as she would do, by filing her dissent, the ratification could not go into effect, because it would not be assented to by all the Allied and Associated Powers.
36G
Even though assented to by Great Britain? Does, my hon. friend claim that the failure of Canada to assent to the reservations would put an end to the whole treaty?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the United States insisted on its resolving words, it would put an end to the ratification, because Great Britain has no right to give consent on behalf of Canada.

Great Britain is a party to the Treaty distinct from Canada. For the purposes of this discussion, Great Britain and Canada are separate nations. The hon. member has ashed what would be the effect of Great Britain assenting to the reservations. Surely the effect would be that Great Britain would remain in the League while Canada vvould leave it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That would not be the
effect, because Canada is in the League. The League has become effective by the ratification of the treaty and by its formal inauguration, and Canada cannot be put out except by her own consent. And even though the situation in Europe might be such as to influence Great Britain to give her consent, if Canada did not assent, ratification could not go into effect. -
On the part of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member has
missed the terms of the resolving clause which I have read. The United States might change its resolving clause so as to accept less than the assent of all the Allied and Associated Powers. Thus far it has not done &o. The resolving clause as it stands at present requires the assent of all the Allied and Associated Powers, and if Canada did not assent ratification could not go into effect.
And the whole treaty would be abortive?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The treaty is in force today. The League of Nations is functioning and is carrying on its work to-day.
The treaty would cease to be effective as regards Canada if she refused to ratify it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not wish to be at cross purposes with my hon. friend. I am sure, he is only anxious to arrive at the truth, and that is also my desire. Let me go back a step. The treaty is in force by the deposit, of ratification, on January 10, by more than three of the great powers and by ^Germany. Under the express terms of

the treaty it becomes effective on the deposit of these ratifications. The treaty going into effect brings the League of Nations into existence. The League was duly organized on January 16 and is operative today. Canada is one of its original members and has all the rights and privileges of every other member of the League. We have every respect for the opinion of the United States, they are entitled to say whether they will or will not come in, but they are not entitled to push us out without our consent, and we cannot be put out otherwise. This is the situation, and it is therefore not a question of our dropping out of the League, for we are already in it. If the United States adopted this clause the misfortune would be that they would come into the League because they had imposed a condition which could not be complied with.

I do not say that Great Britain will or should accept the reservations. I do not for a moment take that position; but if Great Britain should assent to the Lenroot reservations what would be our position under the treaty?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend will turn to the treaty he will see that the contracting party, so far as Canada is concerned, is the British Empire by its representative, His Majesty The King. The British Empire is composed of Great Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, etc., and no one nation of that group has the right to give assent for all. The British Empire's assent, having regard to the constitutional practice that has developed, and in view of our acknowledged status cannot be given without our consent.
That is very debatable.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In order to avoid argument I read from the statement issued by the British Government itself to the British Parliament (the War Cabinet in part) defining our status. Now, when they made that statement, not only to us but to the British Parliament and to all the Dominions, how can it be contended that the Government of Great Britain could give an assent which would bind Canada even although Canada opposed such assent.

It is not a question whether they could, but would they?
Mr: ROWELL: I do not for a moment think that they would give an assent that would bind Canada. I feel absolutely con-

fident that I am speaking well within the mark when I say that the British Government would not think of doing such a thing. No public man in Great Britain would entertain such an idea.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the point of my hon. friend's remarks in regard to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What I deSire to point out, so that the House will appreciate the position, is the fact that should the United States adopt the resolutions now before the Senate, and should the President give his approval, a situation would arise in which the question of the United States coming into the League or not might depend on the action of Canada. It would be a grave responsibility for us, in the face of the serious conditions in Europe and elsewhere, to say that we would not give the necessary consent. But because we -believe, Mr. Speaker, that the question goes to the very basis of Canada's national position, and that her future depends upon it, we could not possibly give that consent.
I have felt it desirable to put the House in the possession of all the facts and I am sure we have the unanimous support of the House in maintaining Canada's status in the League of Nations. The adoption of this resolution by the House will be an intimation to the Government that the House approves the position taken by the Government on this matter of such grave importance to Canada.
The position won for Canada by her soldiers on the field of battle, maintained by her statesmen at the Peace Conference, recognized and established by the ratification of the Treaty of Peace, and the formal inauguration of the League the Government of Canada will maintain. Mr. Speaker, I move the adoption of the resolution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand that this stands for discussion.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will move that the debate be adjourned.

speechtext:
Resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed Resolution of Mr. Burnham:
That in the opinion of this House', it is desirable that to the extent of the jurisdiction of this Parliament a national eight-hour working1 day should be established immediately, subject only to the right of express private contract.

Mr. Speaker, last night when six o'clock was called I was in the act of pointing out to the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) that the existence of shorter hours of labour did not by any means imply a reduction in production, and I was reading a passage from an authority already cited. I desire, Mr. Speaker, to continue the citation.
The last sentence which I gave to the House last night was this:
-that where the human element enter's into production, hour reductions by no means necessarily imply a decrease in output. For instance, the Federal Industrial Commission of 189S made special comparisons between the output of the bituminous coal mines before and after the introduction of the eight-hour day, and found that output even increased under the shorter work day. In Illinois in 1895 and 1896 under the ten-hour system, the average daily output for each mine employee was 2.53 to 3 tons; in 1598, 1899, and 1900, with an eight-hour day, the average output was 3.11 and 3.21 tons, though the proportion of coal mined by machinery was not increased.
In the New England textile industry, also, it was found that the shorter work day consequent upon the enforcement of the ten-hour law improved either the quality or quantity of the output, or both. Similar evidence has been gathered for a number of other industries, showing the beneficial effect of a full day's rest each week. This increase of output through increased efficiency probably largely explains why wages have seldom fallen, but have frequently even risen after a reduction of hours, and why the industries in which wages are highest are often those in which hours are shortest. Practical experience, therefore, gives weight to the old eight-hour league slogan: "Whether you work by the piece or the day, decreasing the hours increases the pay."
Now the principal objection to long hours of labour is that they tend to the breakdown of health, and again I desire to quote the authority in hand, because the mere assertion by one hon. member that a certain condition exists, and the mere contradiction of that assertion by another hon. member, is not going to get us any further with the subject. There is only one way to deal with it, and that is through the investigations which (have been made regarding labour conditions. This authority states:
Under modern industrial conditions such excessive hours of work break down health. Even with short hours the strain of modern industry.

Commons
tation by all these societies and trades unions brought about a general recognition of womenkind in United States.
In Canada very little has been done to improve the condition of the *working woman. In connection with the resolution before the House the conditions as affecting women must be taken into account. The only case in which I have been able to find that action was taken in Canada touching the matter of working hours for women was the appointment of a Royal Commission at Toronto in 1907 to inquire into a dispute between the Bell Telephone Company and its operators. There evidence was given by physicians who declared that if the health of the workers was to be preserved the working day should not be longer than six hours spread over a period of eight hours. So that any legislation which is put on the statute book of this country with regard to the hours of labour must necessarily take into account the conditions under which women work.
Of course, it does not follow that because in some cases women demand a working day of six hours or even eight hours there are not employments in connection with which the hours may be extended over longer periods without impairment of health or safety of the employees.
So far as legislation affecting men is concerned, very little is to be found in United States or in Europe dealing with the matter of hours. The only data that I can find relating to the hours that men should work are in relation to such employments as transportation, street railways, mines and work done under great pressure of air. Representations have been made from time - to time to Federal Governments relating to the hours of men on the ground that the State itself is responsible as one of the parties to the contract, but little has been accomplished.
So far as transportation companies are concerned, the labourers themselves are responsible to some extent for what they have obtained. On the other hand, corporations are quite ready to recognize the demands of the labourers, for the simple reason that in many cases an army of men is involved, and it is expedient for the corporations themselves to have the good-will and cooperation of the labourers. Take the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. They have never had any trouble so far as hours of labour are concerned because their employees constitute an army of three hundred thousand men or more, and it is of vital importance to Canada that there
[.Mr. H. A. Mackie]
should be no tie-up in the work which these men are doing. The company has, therefore, established what is known as a system of runs, so that a man may not necessarily have to work much more than eight hours at a time; and at the end of his run he has an opportunity for rest, enjoyment and repose.
In the matter of mines and tunnels the Provincial legislatures all over the Dominion have passed laws with regard to conditions of labour, it being apparent that these were necessary to the protection of human life. There are, however, cases where a day of even eight hours is too long, and in that respect I wish to quote a number of cases where employment is limited to only one and one-half hours:
The beginning's of such adjustment are, however, to be seen in the laws of New York and New Jersey governing work in compressed air. Even a universal law providing for an eight-hour day is not going to meet the whole situation in the Dominion of Canada. In dealing further with this resolution, the House should take into consideration the question of holidays. As regards Canada, I do not think there is any difficulty now, because both municipalities and provinces have seen, I believe, that the labouring classes get a half day a week at all events; but authorities who have given this matter a great deal of study, claim that the holidays should be increased for

The Labour Conference which was held at Washington took up this question and approved what the authority that I have placed before the House says, because provision has been made in that report to define what is industrial undertaking in one class of work and what is industrial undertaking in another; makes provision for extra long hours in cases of accident or accident being apprehended and also deals with a certain number of cases where the Government is supreme.
