There are, therefore, reksons why this Government should take into consideration legislation along those lines, first because the constitutional question has been dealt with, as I am informed through the medium of the press, and because the International Conference at Washington shows that it is the business of federal authorities to deal with such matters. There was adopted at Washington the following draft dealing with the question of the Treaty of Versailles of 28th June, 1919, and the Treaty of St. Germain of 10th September, 1919:
Article 1.
For the purpose of this Convention, the term Industrial undertaking includes particularly:
(a)	Mines, quarries and other works for the extraction of minerals from the earth.
(b)	Industries in which articles are manufactured, altered, cleaned, repaired, ornamented, finished, adapted for sale, broken up or demolished, or in which materials are transformed, including shipbuilding and the generation, transformation and transmission of electricity or motive power of any kind.
(c)	Construction, reconstruction, maintenance, repair, alteration, or demolition of any building, railway, tramway, harbour, dock, pier, canal, inland waterway, road, tunnel, bridge, viaduct, sewer, drain, well, telegraphic or telephonic installation, electrical undertaking, gas work, waterwork, or other work of construction, as well as the preparation for or laying the foundation of any such work or structure.
(d)	Transport of passengers or goods by road, rail, sea or inland waterway, including the handling of goods at docks, quays, wharves or warehouses, but excluding transport by hand.
24i
The provisions relative to transport by sea and on inland waterways shall be determined by a special conference dealing with employment at sea and on inland waterways.
The competent authority in each country shall define the line of division which separates industry from commerce and agriculture.
This is a very important point in that there is a good deal of apprehension throughout the country that the effect of the declaration .of an eight-hour day will be to infringe upon the rights of the farmer to make private contracts with labourers. Any legislation that is to be passed by this Dominion must be legislation in accord with the principles laid down in this concention and in accord with the principles enunciated in the Treaty of Peace and League of Nations:
Art cle 2.
The working hours of persons employed in any public or private industrial undertaking or in any branch thereof, other than an undertaking in which only members of the same family are employed, shall not exceed eight in the day and forty-eight in the week, -with the exceptions hereinafter provided for.
(a)	The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to persons holding positions of supervision or management, nor to persons employed in a confidential capacity.
(b)	Where by law, custom, or agreement between employers and workers' organizations, or, where no such organizations exist between employers' and workers' representatives, the hours of work on one or more days of the week are less than eight, the limit of eight hours may be exceeded on the remaining days of the week by the sanction of the competent public authority, or by agreement between such organizations or representatives; provided, however, that in no case under the provisions of this paragraph shall the daily limit of eight hours be exceeded by more than one hour.
(c)	Where persons are employed in shifts it shall he permissible to employ persons in excess of eight hours in any one day and forty-eight hours in any one week, if the average number of hours over a period of three weeks or less does not exceed eight per day and forty-eight per week.
Therefore provision must be made in any Federal Act that may be passed for cases where a man may work the maximum of week hours and still not necessarily put in eight hours every day of that week.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The limit of hours of work prescribed in Article 2 may be exceeded in case of accident, actual or threatened, or in case of urgent work to be done to machinery or plant, or in case of ''force majeure," but only so far as may he necessary to avoid serious interference with the ordinary working of the undertaking.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The limit of hours of work prescribed in Article 2 may also be exceeded in those processes which are required by reason of the nature of the process to be carried on continuously by a succession of shifts, subject to the condition that the working hours shall not

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: exceed fifty-six in the week on the average. Such regulation of the hours of work shall in no case affect any rest days which may be secured by the national law to the workers in such processes in compensation for the weekly rest day.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: In exceptional cases where it is recognized that the provisions of Article 2 cannot be applied, but only in. such cases, agreements between workers' and employers' organizations concerning the daily limit of work over a longer period of time, may be given the force of regulations, if the Government, to which these agreements shall be submitted, so decides. The average number of hours worked per week, over the number of weeks covered by any such agreement, shall not exceed forty-eight.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Regulations made by public authority shall determine for industrial undertakings:
(a)	The permanent exceptions that may be "* allowed in preparatory or complementary work
which must necessarily be carried on outside the limits laid down for the general working of an establishment, or for certain classes of workers whose work is essentially intermittent
(b)	The temporary exceptions that may be allowed, so that establishments may deal with exceptional cases of pressure of work.
These regulations shall be made only after consultation with the organizations of employers and workers concerned, if any such organizations exist. These regulations shall fix the maximum of additional hours in each instance, and the rate of pay for overtime shall not be less than one and one-quarter times the regular rate.
An eight-hour day law cannot be passed so summarily as all this. Exceptions must be provided to cover cases where the eight hours may be exceeded. Labour must also be consulted. The International Labour Conference which sat in Washington passed a resolution declaring that before any law was passed relating to labour, or to questions of hours and wages in this or any other country, the labour organizations must be consulted. I believe that is the proper thing to do.
A great deal was said at the International Labour Conference in Washington regarding the question of unemployment. If we are going to deal with the question of hours, which involves the question of wages, we might as well deal also with unemployment and social insurance. I shall not discuss those questions to-night, but the Bill [DOT]ought to deal with them, because these questions are all related to one another.
Before sitting down I should like to draw attention to the resolution itself. I am in favour of the eight-hour day, and to that extent I support the resolution, but the resolution in effect means this: That we should declare it desirable, to the extent of the jurisdiction of this Parliament to have a national eight-hour day established im-

mediately, subject only to the right of express private contract. What is the use of making such a declaration and pass a statute when we leave it open for a telephone operator, for instance, to come along and say to her employer: You are not prohibited from making a contract with me under which I shall be obliged to work sixteen hours a day. If the State is concerned with the welfare of women, and that it is so concerned is evident from' what I have read to you this evening, is it not absolute folly to ask us to put on the statute books of this country a declaration that we have a national eight-hour day, when the principle of that law can be contravened at any time by employer and employee if they choose? If we are going to deal with this question of the eight-hour day at all, it must be from the point of view of the necessity of protecting the individual, whether man, Woman or child, from engaging in a longer working day than eight hours. It may be necessary to legislate that the working hours in some cases should be limited to six or -even four hours a day, but it should not be permitted to an employer to contravene the law by entering into a private contract with his employees. Otherwise, the legislation would stand merely as a farce, and have no force or sanction behind it. A law that merely, says that such and such a'thing shall be established, that provides no penalties for its enforcement, that can be contravened at the will of employer or employee, would not meet the conditions at all. I believe that the resolution as drawn up is weak and futile and does not meet the case. It should be amended for the purpose of meeting the actual conditions as they exist in Canada, so as to come to the relief of the labouring men, or it should not be dealt with at all. In any event, I would hesitate to say that I would support any measure dealing with this question, affecting as it would the whole of Canada, unless the labour organizations are first consulted, because they are familiar with conditions that actually exist and as to which we have very little information.
In conclusion, I wish to say a few words on the attitude of our capitalists and manufacturers. Shortly after the English labour platform was issued, there was such a fear on the part of manufacturers in the Dominion of Canada that they immediately formed a committee composed of the principal manufacturers in the city of Montreal and district to consider what steps should be taken. That committee issued circulars -to all members of Parliament, I believe, and

to all those they thought they could possibly influence, dealing with such questions as co-operation and various other phases of reconstruction that were being much discussed at that time, leading us to believe they were very anxious to do everything they could for labour. They even intimated in their pamphlets and circulars that in some cases labour had not been properly treated. What has beoome of these gentlemen? Nothing has been done. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), then a member of the Cabinet, was chairman of a committee dealing with labour conditions throughout the Dominion, but so far as I know no report was ever made to this House. The Government must have secured data from various sources dealing with conditions throughout the Dominion, but I have not been able to secure any report.
I would point out that there is a great deal to be done by the manfacturers themselves. It is not by legislation alone that you can bring about remedies. There is always some way of evading the law, always some loophole, always something that has not been provided for. The courts might not be in sympathy with the legislation, and very often the labouring classes are not in a position to carry cases to higher courts. What we need in this country is a readjustment of the relations between capital and labour. There must be some disposition on the part of the employers to treat their employees properly, and once they have this disposition the same good relations will prevail between employer and employee in every other industry as prevail in the railway world. You see very few strikes or labour difficulties on the .Canadian Pacific railway. Why is it not possible for other employers of labour to obtain the good will of their employees in the same way? It is not by legislation alone that we can have a perfect understanding between these two forces, And II exhort the men who, at the beginning of the reconstruction period, were issuing pamphlets and letters all over Canada admitting their own shortcomings and promising to do better for labour, to proceed immediately to fulfil those promises. If they do, the necessity for legislation will be dispensed with in a large measure. In any case, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that the resolution as drawn would be null and void as regards any effect which it might have if it were law. I think that a committee should be appointed to consider the matter so that a proper act might be
brought in which would take into consideration all classes of labour in the country under all conditions.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prince, P.E.I.):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It has been intimated that an
opportunity will be given later in the session for the discussion of the question of an eight-hour day, and I shall not take up much time this evening trying to consider the merits of that question on this resolution. My purpose is rather to point out that in dealing with industrial questions it is of the greatest importance that the meanihg of a resolution such as this should be made perfectly clear. Anything either misleading or uncertain in the note sounded by Parliament as to what it projroses to do in regard to this great problem cannot work other than injury to the relations between capital, labour, and the community. This resolution may mean very much or it may mean nothing at all and I desire simply toi ascertain its real significance.
My hon. friend who has just resumed his seat (Mr. H. A. Mackie) points out that the resolution concludes with the words, "Subject only to the right of express private contract." In other words, we are asked to enact an eight-hour day law, with the understanding that individuals notwithstanding shall have the right to enter into express private contracts in the matter of hours. I trust that the mover of the resolution will correct me if I am wrong, but I gather that the meaning of these words is that any individual who employs another may make a contract with him as to his hours of labour on any terms upon which the two are agreed. If that is not the meaning of the words I shall be obliged if the hon. member will make the position clear.

The resolution is on
all fours with the law that applies to the percentage which may be charged in case there is no percentage mentioned in any legal document or instrument. As the hon. gentleman well knows, the principle observed in such cases is that unless there is an .express agreement to the contrary the legal percentage shall be considered as the percentage in the instrument. All this resolution proposes is that it shall be understood that the working day is eight hours unless there is an agreement to the contrary. It is not intended to deprive the working man or any other citizen of the right to make an agreement which he himself considers fair and just, and as for the compulsion that may be behind that, and which the hon. gentleman evidently fears.

I can only say that organized labour will take care of that matter.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: II think that the purpose of my hon. friend, so far as to afford an opportunity to members to express their views on the eight-hour day is concerned, haS been well served. But the resolution itself, worded as it is, will not, I fear, be of any real service to labour. I may frankly say that I am pretty sure that labour would not regard very favourably a resolution of this Parliament approving an eight-hour day witlj the option 'to any one who might care to do so to make any contract he wishes in regard to the hours of labour.	.
If the eight-hour day were enacted without this clause may I ask my hon. friend if there is anything on earth to prevent a man working eighteen hours a day if he chose?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If this Parliament enacted an eight-hour day as labour is demanding in certain industries, it would be necessary to provide certain machinery to see that the law was complied with. In many factories in the country to-day the working day is fixed at eight hours, and if in these factories any effort were made to work men for eighteen hours the owners would be liable to the penalty provided. Simply to pass a pious resolution saying that Parliament is in favour of an eight-hour day but also in favour of allowing the individual the right to make any contract he pleases in regard to hours is to raise a hope which it is impossible to realize.
All this resolution does is to raise a presumption.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend's purpose is served in giving an opportunity for discussion, and in doing so I think he has undoubtedly rendered some service. But in pressing the resolution to a division, I think it would be wise that we should all understand that if we did vote for it we would not be enacting anything one way or the other that is material so far as labour and capital are concerned.	,
There is another clause in the resolution to which some attention should be devoted before a vote is asked upon it. The resolution refers to the extent of the jurisdiction of this Parliament.
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that to the extent of the jurisdiction of this Parliament a national eight-hour working day should be established immediately

There is an old-time saying, Mr. Speaker, that it is not a wise thing to buy a pig in a poke; and I think my hon. friend will agree with me that it is equally unwise to legislate in the dark. Without knowing what the jurisdiction of Parliament is on this question of an eight-hour day, whether Parliament has a wide jurisdiction or no jurisdiction at all, I submit that it would be unwise to pass a resolution of this kind. My purpose, when I rose, was to point this fact out to the President of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) and to express the hope that when he speaks on the resolution he wall inform the House whether the Government has considered the question of ascertaining what the jurisdiction of this Parliament is in the matter of eight-hour day legislation. I think it is important that that phase of the subject should be made perfectly clear before any considerable discussion takes place in Parliament on the eight-hour day problem. The one thing we are interested to know is, what is the jurisdiction, of this Parliament in the matter. When we have ascertained that, we should proceed to the next step and say how far we think this Parliament should go under such jurisdiction as it may have. If the Government has not already taken steps to ascertain the proper jurisdiction of Parliament, I think it-would be in the interests of labour and capital and, indeed, of all classes, that this should be done and that-the House should be informed accordingly.

Canada at
the present time, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, is trying to devise ways and means of increasing production and retaining its men on the farms, and this resolution, it seems to me, would have the effect of luring boys from the rural districts. It must be remembered that half of our population reside on the farms. It may be said that this has nothing to do with the farmers, but I do not see how we can deal with this matter without considering how it will affect the farmers. The young man is going to try and get the largest wages he can and to work the shortest hours. We are all doing that; we are all trying to make the most out of the shortest time. How the farmers are going to secure help to work twelve or thirteen hours a day when there is a legal eight-hour day is something I cannot understand. That is one of the principal reasons why there is this great exodus from the farms to the cities. Too many of our young men-and middle-aged men too-are going to the cities. Ask them the question and they will tell you that they are going

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
from the farm to the city because they cannot work the farms themselves and they cannot get help. I think that there should be no legislation put on the statute book at the present time that will take men away from the farms to the cities. Many men I know would be quite willing to stay on the farm if they could get help. But th£ 'farmer and his wife have perhaps got too old to work the farm; they cannot get help, and they are forced to give up the farm and go to the* city. As soon as the war started wages became extremely high, young men went to the city, and you cannot get them to return to the farm.
I am not in favour of any class of men working extremely long hours. There are some kinds of work at which six, and probably four hours would be enough, but if these industries can hire men to work for whatever hours they wish, why should we put a law of this kind on the statute book? We are told that it is only for the factories, offices and shops. If that is so why not say that they can hire them for as many hours as they choose the same as the farmers can? We are told that the farmer can hire his help for whatever hours he wishes. That is all very well; I suppose he 9 p.m. can, but the question is to get the men. Why do farmers work such long hours?-they are asked by the people in the cities and towns of Canada. City people are howling about the high cost of living, and I quite agree that it is very high. Farm products in many cases are high, but I want to say that the very moment you enact the eight-hour day you are going to increase the cost of living. If we attempt to work on the farms even ten hours a day we will reduce, in the first place, the production of milk and butter to the extent of one-sixth at least. When I was on the faim we tried to milk the cows at seven o'clock in the morning and at seven at night. We did that in order to milk them at .a regular hour, twelve hours apart. If we wanted to have less milk or to put the cows dry we would milk them at intervals, probably sixteen hours apart. It is impossible to produce the same amount of milk, butter, cheese, wheat or grains of all kinds if we are going to have an eight-hour day. The difference between the farm and the shop and factory is this: They can get a supply of men and they can put on different'shifts to keep the work going, but who could say that a farmer in this Dominion could hire two sets of men? It is impossible, you cannot get one, let alone getting two. Are you going to tie
down the farmer, who has worked for fifty or sixty years twelve or fourteen hours a day, to an eight-hour day? If he is willing to give the wages to get men to work eight hours a day in the field must he and his wife work twelve and fourteen hours in order to feed the stock and milk the cows? This is a great injustice to the farmers of the country. If we want to put legislation on the statute book to take more men off the farm we could not devise anything more calculated to bring that about than the measure suggested by this resolution, and if we adopt it we are going to be up against a greater difficulty than many of us are aware of.
I realize, the same as my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) and many other members of this House, that there is a great clamour for short hours but the people living in the cities, as well as others, should not do anything that is going to injure the great basic industry of Canada, which is agriculture. II feel satisfied that many thousands will leave the farm if, as a result of this Bill being placed on the statute book, they cannot get farm labour. As I said before, a young man going out and seeking a job will say: I will look where I can get the most pay and the shortest hours. That will not be on the farm. With all respect to the labour men, I believe as the hon. member for Peterborough said, that they should be allowed to hire at whatever hours they wish, and I believe that that view is shared by many hon. members of this House. Therefore, the law would be no good; as the hon. the leader of the. Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, the law would be a farce if it did not bind anybody. If you put a law on the statute -book and say that we must stick to the eight-hour day you will ruin the farmers whereas if you put it the other way and say that the manufacturers or the employer can hire as he wishes the law will be ineffective. There are jobs that are so hazardous and extremely hard that four, six or eight hours would be sufficient for them, but out in the open air, where the conditions are favourable and conducive to health, there is nothing to hinder a man from working ten or twelve hours a day. We see masons, carpenters and other mechanics clamouring for eight hours a day instead of nine or ten. Any one who says that you can get as much work done in eight hours as in ten does not know what he is talking about. We have had too much of this practice of limiting the amount of work that a man can do in a day. Where

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: a man could probably lay double the amount of brick that another man could he is restrained, he is not allowed to work to his capacity, but he must only lay so many brick. There is no encouragement for the man who is willing to work and make an honest living. I would ask the members of this House to remember that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada, and that if you support this Bill you will do more to take the boys off the farm than could possibly be done by any other measure that could be brought before this House.

Mr. Speaker, I have always been a farmer and I know the conditions under which work on the farm is carried on. I think that this measure to limit the day's work to eight hours is one of the most dangerous that could be brought before this House, and I am of the opinion that before it is adopted it should receive the most careful consideration. The agricultural industry represents a production of $1,500,000,000, an amount which exceeds the production of all the other industries in Canada. Such an important industry as that of agriculture should be given due consideration and any measure affecting it so vitally as this one does should not be hastily dealt with. The House would do well to bear in mind the fact that four and a half per cent of the farmers and seventeen per cent of the farm labourers have gone to the cities. Why? Because of shorter hours and greater pay. A measure, such as is now proposed, to legalize the eight-hour day would be- very dangerous from the point of view of agriculture. There is not a farmer who could get any hired help, no matter what price he offered, because	the	men
would have gone to the	cities for
shorter hours and still larger wages. Eight hours a day is very short. For instance, how can you get a crop in if you start at eight o'clock in the morning and finish at five in the evening? How are you to take your harvest off within such working hours? And how are you going to get your seeding done? I know I could never get. my farm work done within tho'se hours, and I would very much like to see some of those men who are advocating the eight-hour day go out on the farm; undoubtedly -it would teach them a lesson. It is an utter impossibility to talk of farming on an eight-hour day. I never was an advocate of long hours-I never wept into the field earlier than seven o'clock in the morning, and I always left at six o'clock in the 
evening. If a man cannot stand that many hours in the field he is no good at farming; he should become an inmate of some charitable institution.
I think it would have been better had this matter not been brought forward. Factory men are well looked after by their local unions; and I say, let farmers hire as they can. There is no doubt that at the present time no farmer or his help has to work excessively long hours, but if this law goes into force it will'cause trouble. If you hire a man for a month, six months, or a year, he will turn round and tell you that he has to work only eight hours a day, and if you want him to work beyond those hours you will have to pay him, not regular wages, but, I suppose, time and-a-half. We see that in connection with railroads and business concerns, and it is safe to assume that we farmers would be treated in the same way.
Our farmers do not work for fun-I certainly never did-and I want to tell you that just as soon as you pass this Bill your cost of living will rise fifteen or twenty per cent higher- and God knows it is high enough already. It cannot be otherwise. Again, look at the European nations; there is not one of them but has a twelve or fourteen-hour day. How are you going to compete with them? We will have 1878 conditions back again, when you could not sell a pound of butter for more than ten cents. I myself have sold oats at nineteen cents a bushel, and potatoes at fifty-five cents a bushel.
I, trust, gentlemen, that before voting in favour of this resolution'you will look into it very carefully. As a member of this House I am just as anxious for the welfare of our. people as anyone, but if I voted for an eight-hour day I believe I would be voting against the best interests of the Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I understood yesterday from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) that this eight-hour question would be discussed at a later date, and I [DOT] had no idea it was coming up to-day; in fact, it is not on the Order Paper so far as I could see.
The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that to the extent of the jurisdiction of this Parliament

Before pressing a resolution of this kind, would it not be wise for us to find out what is the jurisdiction of Parliament?
I understand from certain legal authorities that there is a difference of opinion as to

whether that jurisdiction is within the province's or the Dominion. Therefore, I am sorry that my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. (Burnham) insists on pressing his resolution to a vote to-night.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman, who does he suppose has jurisdiction outside the provinces?
Outside the provinces?
Yes. Are there no lands outside the provinces?
Those lands are worked principally by the wolves; we have not much jurisdiction over them.
You said we could have no jurisdiction.
I agree absolutely with my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best) that labour is perfectly safe
Oh, oh.

to he left alone to
regulate its hours. Employers fully realize that the labour unions are quite capable of making arrangements as to the hours of labour in the various industries. Of recent years, so far as I know, there ha$ been no trouble on that score. One business, on account of the work being very concentrated, may require very short hours of labour. We can leave it to the employers and employees to decide whether a man can do his best working four, six, eight or ten hours a day.
I think it would be a mistake for Parliament to pass a resolution of this kind, which commits us to legislation, until we know just exactly what jurisdiction we possess. As I said before, I think it is perfectly safe to leave the regulation of this matter for the industries concerned. I know industries that work their men in some branches in four-hour shifts only. I know of other industries where the shifts are six hours, and others where they are eight hours, depending on the amount of concentration required during the hours of labour. In some industries a man can work just as well' ten hours a day as eight hours. Farming is an industry, as mentioned by my hon. friend from Peterboro, that has always worked ten or twelve hours, it being a type of labour that does not call for excessive concentration. If you watch farmers you will observe that as a rule they work very leisurely except at certain times of the year; for instance, during harvesting and haying, when for a few days they may work at considerable pressure if
the weather is threatening or there is some other reason for haste. Under such circumstances you very seldom see men refuse to work even at night to save the harvest in the field. I do not think we should interfere with arrangements such as those. We have got to be guided by circumstances, and farming is very much of an industry, indeed, in this country-an industry of such vital importance that we should not attempt to interfere with its hours of labour in any shape or form.
If it is provided by statute that the length of the working day shall be eight or even ten hours, the probabilities are that men who are employed by the day and not by the year will work only during the hours specified by the statute. In that case, work on the farm would be thrown out of gear; because on the farm some of the men work certain hours and others have to work, or do work, longer. I cannot help thinking that it would be a great mistake for this House to adopt this resolution committing us to an eight-hour day for the whole of Canada. * It hasi been very well said that so far as our industries are concerned we compete with many other countries. Of course, if all -the countries which are signatories to the League of Nations accepted the eight-hour day; and it became universal, enabling all countries to compete on the same basis-except perhaps, in the matter of wages-it would be a different matter. But II think it would be a great mistake to adopt a resolution of 'this kind until we know exactly what our jurisdiction is and until we have discussed the matter thoroughly from the standpoints of the various industries throughout the country. I hope that the hon. member will - not press his resolution to a vote; if he does, I shall toe obliged to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, in many respects I have a good deal of sympathy with the resolution. Labour has had the heavy end of the work of our country for many years. It is thought by many that the hours of labour could be reduced to the advantage of the general industrial community. But before giving my view upon that question I wish to touch, upon the point raised by the member for* North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) with regard to jurisdiction.
As I understand it, this House has not the jurisdiction to carry into effect legislation based upon such a resolution as that which has been submitted by the member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). The jurisdiction in the matter is confined largely
o78

to the provinces. But I think that we would go a long way toward meeting the view of my hon. friend and giving an example to the provinces in connection with legislation which they might later introduce if we adopted a resolution providing that in all Government contracts of every description, whether carried out as piece work or as work sub-let to contractors, it be stipulated that *eight hours a day shall be considered the legal working day for the men engaged in these enterprises. I have not studied the matter from the legal aspect, nor am I in a position to do so; but I believe that this would he a good step to take.
II do not think it would be any infringement upon the liberty of the subject or work hardship to any contractor or working man if, in accordance with the last few' words of my hon. friend's resolution, the right to arrange for longer hours under certain circumstances should be accorded. There might be a case where an employee would be willing to work ten hours a day in order to bring about the completion of a contract at a given time, provided, of course, that the employee was recompensed accordingly. The proviso in the latter part of the resolution, therefore, is quite ini order.
I believe that it is not possible for all industries to comply with any regulation establishing the length of the working day at eight hours. There are processes of manufacture in this country to which such a law could not be very readily applied. Six or eight hours of labour in certain callings takes far more out of a man than ten or twelve at some lighter work. I see a good deal of force, therefore, in the argument put forward by the member for Duff-erin (Mr. Best) and member for Carleton (Mr. Boyce) with regard to the farming community.
I did not hear the address of the member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) on this subject and I do not know whether he made any allowances for weather conditions -these sometimes prevent the labourer from carrying on any work on the farm. For instance, in harvest time no work can be done in the field when the weather is wet. I am sure the member for Peterborough does not wish to suggest that if there are two or three wet days in succession the eight-hour day provision shall he considered as having been fulfilled even though no work at all was done. If, therefore, his resolution called for a forty-eight hour week instead of an eight-hour day, it would be better. For instance, one day might he wet and the next day fine, and the farm labourer could put in twelve

or fourteen hours on a fine day if it were necessary to do so in order to save'the crop, instead of saying: Well, it rained yesterday and I could not work, but it must be counted as an eight-hour day; and to-day I will only work eight hours. In fact, I am doubtful, as I have said, whether such legislation could be applied to the farming community; nor do I think it is desirable that it should. We should differentiate between the different industries. I come from an industrial city where from eight to ten . thousand workmen are employed, and our factories are endeavouring to adhere very closely to the principle of the eight-hour day. In fact, the eight-hour day is actually in vogue in some of the best factories in our community; so that without legal enactment of any kind, labour and capital have in these cases agreed that eight hours is the workingman's day. But to other industries the principle could not be applied. Suppose a man is running a single machine which has cost his employer $15,000 or $20,000, and which represents the work of fifty, or, perhaps one hundred men under the old system of hand labour. The work that used to be done by the sledge hammer and the multiplication of sledge hammers is now done by a single machine which, when a button is pushed, strikes a twenty-ton blow. When that machine, therefore, comes to a standstill a large amount of capital comes to a standstill; and if the eight-hour day principle were applied to the industry in connection with which that machine was operated it might be necessary to run two shifts of eight hours each, perhaps even three shifts, in order that that machine might be worked to full capacity. If the eight-hour day had been in vogue during the war, how many of our requirements for munitions could have been fulfilled? Not very many. It was necessary to get the very highest amount of production, and that cannot be done-by limiting the hours of labour to eight hours a day in all callings. But I am favourable to the eight-hour day;
I believe that the system should be brought into effect in Canada so far as we are able to bring it into effect. As I understood the President of the Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) to say, it is important that in legislating for an eight-hour day for Canada as a whole we have some regard to what the other nations of the world are going to do about it. We in Canada cannot, if we establish an eight-hour day, compete with our neighbours to the south if they work on a basis of ten hours a day. If Germany is going to work twelve, fifteen or sixteen hours, to say

nothing of Japan, China and other countries which underpay their labour and exact very long hours, the eight-hour day cannot bring about the best results. An international arrangement between labour and capital throughout the whole civilized world is the final consummation for the eight-hour day proposition.

Do I understand the
hon. gentleman to say that the Chinese must agree to this first?

I did not say so, but I say it is desirable that all nations so far as possible should agree to it. I hope we are a little more advanced than the Chinese, but they are coming up pretty fast and they -are competing with us, and we must have some attention to what is going oil in outside nations. That is the point I wish to make, and it should be taken into consideration. I am not clear as _to what a day's work should consist of, but it should really consist of a certain product. A certain product should be turned out in a day's work. I know the hon. member for West Peterborough has a great regard for the ten commandments, one of which says: Six days shalt thou labour and do all thy work. Whether we can do that in an eight-hour day or not, I am not quite clear, but we are commanded to do six day's work in the week whether we are engaged as labourers or otherwise. Whether we are working with our hands, or our heads, it makes little difference, everybody in this country is supposed to work for his daily bread. Labour has thought-and I think justly-that they have been oppressed somewhat in the past in being compelled to work too long hours. Therefore, while I have a very broad and strong sympathy with the resolution of my hon. friend,-and, in fact, I am personally committed to it, but that does not amount to much, because I am only a humble member of the House-I should like to see a large measure of legislation along the lines I have indicated.

Is
there a commandment that forbids one from robbing a man of his health or killing him by making him run a fifteen thousand dollar machine?

Some of those expensive machines are run with less individual effort than is expended on very much lighter work, and take very much less out of the operator than does some very much lighter work. What is necessary is that the man should be very careful not to
get his hand or leg or something of that kind into the machine. It requires constant attention and great activity on his part to see that he does not get hurt. The mere pressing of a button and stopping the machine when the operation is completed could be performed by a child, but it re-ouires an expert man to know when the piocess is completed. I suppose the hon member is aware that the Workmen's Compensation Act is in force in Ontario, and if any manufacturer has a man injured in his factory, he has to pay very heavily, and, T think, rightly so. Therefore, the workingman is very well protected against accidents that may occur in factories, and an employer is obliged to pay what is considered a fair recompense to a man for the loss of any member of his body or for being maimed in any way whatever.

Mr. Speaker, I think it would be a great mistake to adopt this resolution just at present and to say that an eight-hour day was the legal working day for the labourers of this country. I Lave, however, no objection to the eight. hour day. My heart goes out to the labouring man of Canada and, in fact of the world, who works eight hours or ten hours a day or whatever number of hours a day he has to work and works hard. If present commercial and financial conditions in Canada will allow a citizen of this country to make a good living by working eight hours a day, aye, by working only six hours a day, then I say: Go to it, and let that be the working day, but I do not think circumstances will permit that. Never before in Canada were we,looking and waiting and asking more anxiously for greater production, and I do not think I am saying anything wide of the fact when I say that there never before was a time when people wanted to do less and get more for the little they did. A few weeks ago I noticed that the Post Office Department of the United States sent out what one might call questionnaires to 290,000 different farmers asking them what that department could do to assist the farming community in the way of greater production or in getting labour on their farms. A -short time ago they had received some forty odd thousand replies, of which over ninety per cent, if my memory serves me aright, indicated the intention of either quitting the farm altogether or curtailing it to such an extent as to permit the farmer to run it with his own labour. They said in their replies that the reason for their intention

was that they could not compete with the high prices paid in the city and the short hours. We all know that labour in this city, as in every city not only of Canada but of this continent, is shouting about the high cost of living. Some speakers have already said that they would not object to the eight-hour day if it were not applied to the farmer. I am not speaking particularly in the interest of the farmer; I am convinced that the farmer cannot operate successfully with an eight-houi day; but if the eight-hour day were applied generally in the industries in cities and towns, what would be the result? Why, you would not have in a county a baker's dozen of young men on the farms. Just last night, I happened to look over the municipal statistics for the province of Ontario, and according to the census statistics sent out by the department, from the end of 191) to the end of 1917 there were 28,000 fewer people living in the rural municipalities. That means that 28,000 people had left the rural municipalities and. I suppose, had gone to the cities where probably they could get $6 for eight hours' work. Just in conclusion, 1 would , say that I am heartily in sympathy with the very shortest hours of labour under which the work this country may be carried on successfully, but I do not think it would redound, physically, mentally or in any other way, to the benefit of Canada for our men to work six hours a day and play eighteen. Why, when Adam was put out of the Garden of Eden he was told "By the sweat of thy brow shalt thou earn thy bread," but nobody wants to sweat these days. While I am in sympathy with the labouring man, I think it should be left to the employers and the men themselves to work the hours they choose. If Canada could carry on effectively on a six-hour day, I would not object; but under present conditions, not only in Canada but throughout the world, I do not think that is possible. If this resolution is pressed to a vote, I do not think it would be wise for us to say by our action in this House'that an eight-hour day should be the standard working day all over Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
speechtext:
The hon. member for West
Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) has brought before the House a very important subject, and it lias been the means of bringing out a very interesting and instructive debate. I would indulge the hope that in accomplishing that my hon. friend had done all that 
he could expect to accomplish at the present stage. I do not quite see what good end is to be served by dividing the House on this matter. His resolution, naturally enough, does not enact anything. It expresses a broad general opinion in favour of the eight-hour day, and most of us, I think, are prepared in general terms to subscribe to that. I quite realize that for most occupations eight hours is a fair day's work, and if a man can avoid working more than that, in most occupations, it would be better for himself and I hope better for the community. But we^have already declared in general terms that we subscribe to the eight-hour idea. It has been included, as the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has mentioned, in the Peace Treaty which we approved a year ago. So we.have already done in effect what my hon. friend asks us to do now, and that is to give a broad general expression of approval of the eight-hour system. It seems to me that before we can go beyond that we ought to have something more definite before us. We ought to have the Bill, because a man may be in favour of the principle of an eight-hour laiw, but when you come to apply it in detail, it may not be so easily worked out as some of us would like it to be. I do not think that my hon. friend by pressing this to a division can get one step further than he has already gone. We have already declared our approval of the eight-hour idea, and that is all my hon. friend wants us to do here. The President of the Privy Council in discussing another matter to-day told us that as a consequence of the discussions and conferences that had taken place rising out of the Peace Treaty the obligation rested upon every government that was a party to the International Labour Conference to bring forward legislation in favour of the eight-hour law, and of course it follows that he must bring forward a measure of that kind this session, so far as it is wdthin the competence of this Parliament to deal with the matter. With that assurance^ for that was the effect of the statement of the President of the Privy Council, I do not see what good we can accomplish by dividing the House at the present time.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman practically to identify my resolution with the statement made by the President of the Privy Council? .

It is not for me to put interpretations on the statement of the President of the Privy Council, except as they occur to everybody present. I do not

think I have misstated his position. I asked him to-day what would be the consequences of this Labour Conference, and he replied that every government that participated in the Conference is under an obligation to submit to its Parliament the results of the conclusions arrived at. Very well; the conclusion arrived at is favourable to the eight-hour' law.
Hear, hear.
And the President of the Privy Council told us in effect that the Government would be prepared to carry out its obligation. '
Certainly, and we will vote for the measure.

I am a little more
patient than my hon. friend. I am willing to wait a little while until the Bill is before us in all its details.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I
would care ic give any opinion on the extent of jurisdiction which this House might have in this matter. Generally speaking, one would think that under the British North America Act, it was a matter primarily for the provinces to deal with. Whether our new relationship in the League of Nations gives the matter an international or a broadly national aspect is another question. There is no precedent to guide us, for these conditions have but newly arisen. However, the mover of this resolution has- guarded against any question of jurisdiction arising, by limiting his resolution to the extent of the jurisdiction which this House may have, and so I regard it more or less as calling for an expression of general opinion in regard to the eight-hour day.
I think reason is largely on the side of the eight-hour day. A day's work may sometimes be too short, but many a day's work has been made too long in the past. Personally I think eight hours is a fair and reasonable working day, and I believe that in most instances you would get just as much work done in eight hours as in nine or ten. Making the working day eight hours would not limit production so much as do certain feelings which sbmetimes exist among working men. In some parts of Canada, for instance, among members of certain organizations, not labour organizations, but which have among their membership some labour men, there has been an absolute propaganda against production. That is the kind of influence we must be
in a position to fight, and if we want to be in a position to fight unreasonable demands such as those for a six-hour or a seven-hour day, we must be in a clean position ourselves; we must give our opinion in favour of the things which are fair and the things which are right. I believe the eight-hour day is a fair and' reasonable proposition, and I think it would be a mistake if this House declared itself as being opposed to it.
I think it would be giving the wrong sort of leadership to the country, and would create feelings of unrest which would not tend to increase production. We have had a Factory Act in Alberta for the last year or two, which among other provisions limits the hours of work in many industries to eight. The Act has worked fairly well; there may have been some difficulties, but on the whole we.have carried on, and I believe that with the better feeling and cooperation that came when labour was given this reasonable working day, we got greater production than when we forced the men to work longer hours. The eight-hour day will give them more time for recreation, self-improvement, and for looking after those interests which a man must attend to outside of his ordinary business. I have no hesitation in stating that I am in favour of the principle of the eight-hour day, but I realize that it would not be wise to make the law operative in some - industries for some tihie to come, until they have got on a basis where they could carry on successfully under these new conditions.
Mi-. ALPHONSE YERVILLE (St. Denis): Mr. Speaker, this is not a new question in this House, although to many members it may be new. An eight-hour measure .was presented to the House in 1911, and got its second reading and was considerd in committee, but the dissolution of the House prevented the Bill from going through the Senate. In 1912 no Bill was presented; tliere was a change of Government. I presented that Bill myself in 1911 and was in hopes that it would become law. Nothing was done in 1913. In 1914 the war broke out. This resolution proposes nothing new. 1 believe my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) supported the Bill when it was before the House on the occasion I speak of, and he either said that it did not go far enough or that it went too far. Ii my memory serves me well,' I am inclined to think 'his opinion was -that it went too far. II think we should bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, the important fact- that any legislation that may be introduced by any gov-

ei-nment in regard to the -working classes should pay due respect to the -welfare of the sound element in labour. As we all know, there are two elements of supreme consequence in the life of the civilized world to-day: One which is seeking to bring about destruction, and the other which is endeavouring to be constructive. And I' think that the sound element of labour will assuredly win in the end. They are doing so in this country and also in the United States. Any legislation, therefore, which can be enacted for the relief of those who are now asking for an eight-hour working day will serve to create a better feeling and understanding in the country and will do more towards the reconciliation of classes and the restoration of peace than anything else. I think that any one who reads what is transpiring in this country and elsewhere will agree with me when I say that the unsound element-if I may classify certain people under that term-are not very numerous, although they are very noisy and will drag along with them large numbers of men who follow them inconsiderately, not really knowing where they are going. On the other hand, the sound element has been fighting to counteract the influence oif destructive agencies and I believe that a great deal of success has attended the efforts of those men in the community who have tried to bring about peace and goodwill. It is no more than right that every consideration should be given to this question, which is one of the most important that could be brought before Parliament. My hon. friend from Brantford made the statement that the principle could be applied to public works. That was exactly the object of the eight-hour Bill of 1911. I am not prepared to say just how far the Government can go in - its jurisdiction; but I am confident that during the present session -we shall have a measure of this nature that will furnish an opportunity to discuss the merits of the eight-hour day. At the present time I do not think I need enter into that question.

I feel myself somewhat in the position of the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), I had been in hopes that the debate would not come on at this time, because I have a lot of data in connection with the eight-hour day from different corporations proving that they have been more successful, and that their output has been even greater, under an eight-hour day than it was when they worked ten and twelve hours a day. Those data, I regret to say, I have not with me at this moment, and I

cannot give to the subject that degree of justice which I should otherwise have been in a position to give to it. I cannot agree with t.he hon. member for North Oxford in the statement that labour organizations should look after the working hours for labouring men. Practically speaking, the labour organizations take care of the union men of the country, but there is a great army of labouring men and women who do not belong to any organization. I should therefore like to see some legislation put on tiie statute book affording those people whose occupations do not entitle them to membership in labour organizations some degree of protection. There seems to be an opinion, almost an apprehension, on the part of some members that Canada may be in the lead in enacting an eight-hour day; but there is no ground for this assumption, as the following extracts in regard to the eight-hour day movement abroad will clearly show:
United States

In the United States, federal legislation providing for an eight-hour day in certain Government contract work existed prior to 1892, hut it was vaguely worded and uncertain in effect. An Act of 1890 provided for a straight eight-hour day for labourers and mechanics employed hy the Federal Government or by contractors or sub-contractors on public works.
Twenty-nine states of the union have enacted legislation reducing to eight hours the working day for employees in public employment or in private employment on contract work for national, state or municipal governments. At the end of 1918, fourteen states had enforced the eight-hour day for miners and eight states had forbidden the employment of men in smelting operations for longer than eight hours per day. Eleven states provide for an eight-hour day for men employed in industries involving special hazards.'
By agreements between employers and workmen or hy the award of an official labour adjustment body, an eight-hour day has been put in force in several industries. The members of the International Typographical Union won a concession on this point in 1906. An eight-hour day and forty-four week is the rule for the greater part of the building trades. The American Woollen Company, the largest of its kind in the United States, the United States Steel Corporation, the Ford Automobile Company and other large industrial establishments have adopted the basic eighf-hour day. Australia-
In Australia hours of labour are limited bylaw in the ease of factories and shops, the general working week being forty-eight hours, and this period has been standardized in most occupations. A strong demand has now arisen for a week of forty-eight hours.
New Zealand-
In New Zealand the Factories Act, 1908, made the forty-eight hour week legal in all places of occupation where two or more persons are employed in the preparation, of goods for trade or sale.

France-
In April of the present year, an Aot was passed by the French Parliament providing that the working hours of all workers shall not exceed eight a day or forty-eight a week, or an equivalent limit over some period other than a week. The application of this principle to * particular industries and localities is entrusted to the government.
Italy-
A working day of eight hours has been introduced recently in the metal, engineering and shipbuilding industries, and in the principle textile trades in Italy. An unanimous decision by the agriculturists and representatives of agricultural workers was reached in April, 1919, whereby the hours of work for agricultural labourers hired by the day were to be reduced to eight. Overtime was to be allowed under certain conditions at special rates.
I had an opportunity of going through the country with the Industrial Commission last year, and in the great majority of places we visited we found a demand for a shorter working day based on the desire for more leisure and energy to devote to things of life other than work, and a general approval of employers in this regard-in our report we mentioned such industries as farming, fishing and logging. These three were mentioned as being industries in which it is almost impossible to adopt an eight-hour day. I hope this motion will not be voted down. I expect that the question will come up in the House in the shape of a Bill and I will be prepared to say a great deal more on it than I have to-night. But if it comes to a vote I can assure you 1 am going to vote in favour of this resolution.
Mr. WILLIAM D. EULER (North Waterloo) : Mr. Speaker, last year I asked the question of the Government as to whether they intended to enact eight-hour legislation. At that time a member of the Government gave the leply to the House that this Parliament had no power to enact such legislation. Since that time the principle has been embodied in the Treaty of Peace, and later still it was endorsed by the Canadian representatives to the Industrial Conference held at Washington. In the early days of this session I again placed upon the Order Papei a question as to whether the Government was still of the opinion that Parliament had no power to deal with this question, and also, if it was no longer of that opinion, whether it intended at this session to enact the eight-hour day. Up to this time no reply has been given to that question. During the debate this afternoon the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) who was one of the delegates to the Industrial Conference at Washington made the statement that the eight-hour day principle was endorsed at the session of the Conference by a vote of something like 90 to 2. He made the further statement that if a resolution of that kind was carried by a vote of at least two-thirds of the members of the Conference the Governments of the respective countries were obligated to translate that action into legislation. I inquired of the minister this afternoon whether it was the intention of the Government to bring in legislation to enact the eight-hour day in Canada and I received the reply, as perhaps most of the members of the House know, that there is still some question as to the power of Parliament to enact such legislation. It seems to me that the Government has had sufficient time since last year to. come to some decision on this matter. Perhaps it is an uncharitable thing to say but the thought that is present in my mind is that the Gov-10 p.m. eminent is evading the issue or perhaps, in other words, is doing what it has done before, especially with reference to the daylight saving matter- it is passing the buck. It is true that the motion as framed has po binding effect. It still leaves it open to the men and the employers to bargain as to the number of hours they desire to work in a day. That may be quite true but it does affirm the general principle that in the opinion of the Canadian Parliament eight hours of honest work should under ordinary circumstances, constitute a full day's labour. With that sentiment I am heartily in accord. I am free to admit that in certain activities, such as farming and others which might be named, it would not be possible to conduct these activities on the basis of an eight-hour day, but I do believe that in industrial centres, such as the city which I have the honour to represent, the city of Kitchener, in many industries and perhaps in most, where the men must time their actions according to the demands of the machines which they serve, and which put in many instances an intense strain upon them, eight hours of real, strenuous, hard, faithful labour is sufficient for any man. I would also affirm that, while I believe that at the present time, succeeding the conclusion of the war, production is more necessary than ever it was before, yet man. after all, if he is not simply to consider living as existing, is entitled to just a little more than the hours of labour and the hours of sleep. I believe he might very well divide his life up into three shifts,

 eight hours of labour, eight hours of recreation and eight hours of sleep. Fpr that rea-

son I am going to vote for the motion if it is pressed to a division. Although it does not bind the employer and employee definitely, it does affirm the one principle that eight hours of real, hard work, constitutes a sufficient day of labour. While that principle has already been affirmed by the League of Nations and by the Industrial Conference in Washington, such an affirmation coming from the representatives of the people in the Canadian Parliament, will constitute a good deal of an object lesson and serve as an ideal for both employer and employee.

Mr. Speaker, the motion under discussion moved by my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) is certainly one the principle of which has engaged the attention of the people not only of Canada but of all the civilized countries to a very great extent for many years past. Organized labour has been agitating for something of this nature for quite a number of years. In many occupations, when labour organizations were first formed, it was absolutely necessary that some reforms should be made in the conditions under which they were operating at that time. I have listened to the discussion to-night, and the question to my mind is one of such great importance that I question very much the wisdom of hastily arriving at a decision on this resolution at the present time. Undoubtedly there will be other legislation dealing with it as it is now' embodied in the Treaty of Peace and the question will clearly have to be dealt with by nations which are members of the League of Natiohs.
We have all heard it stated repeatedly that since the war has ended there is a good deal of insanity prevalent throughout the world. If there was ever a time in the history of the world when people required their sanity to enable them to carry on it is at this time, and under the conditions which have to be met. During the years prior to the war there was a worldwide movement from the rural districts to the industrial centres. This movement attained such proportions that it was predicted by far-Seeing students of economics who had studied the question very closely that the day would soon be reached when this world was likely to find itself up against starvation.
The removal during the war of hundreds of millions of men from the productive activities of life to that of destruction has brought about a condition of affairs that 
to my mind is most serious. I am firmly convinced that should the world experience a short crop during the present year starvation will be experienced in many countries, and many people will suffer terrible privations as a consequence of the very low food supply. _
I do not like to contemplate the effect that such legislation will have on agriculture, it having been already referred to. Personally, I firmly believe that the fixing of an eight hour day will ultimately benefit those who .remain in agriculture, those who persist to the end, just as .much as it will benefit those more immediately affected. I cfnmly believe that those who to-day are agitating for such legislation are going to defeat the very object they now have in view, that is, to reduce the cost of living. It is absolutely impossible to bring that about and do what they are now urging this Parliament and the Parliaments of other countries to do.
We have heard a great deal about organized labour, but the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Harrison) has referred to the fact that we have in. this country a tremendous army of unorganized labour. And, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out again that it was somewhat significant that last year we had an International Industrial Conference in the Victoria Museum building which was supposed to deal with all such questions of labour and industry as we are discussing to-night and if possible find a solution for them, but at which this great army of unorganized labour was not represented, neither was the great basic industry of agriculture. I ask. Sir, whether that was a proper means by which to arrive at a satisfactory solution of this question?
An eight-hour day seems ideal, and under most conditions it is. As a matter of fact, it is much longer than a great many people work to-day. I could not help wondering whether the hon. member for Peterboro would compel some people to work eight hours a day, as he refers to this as a National Eight-hour Day. The Government of this country for many years past have established a national working day of much fewer hours. How many people do you suppose work eight hours a day in the Civil Service? Why, a whole army of them never think of working that many hours, and the Government by legislation made this possible many years ago,-they blazed the way so far as this agitation is concerned. But certain people doing business for this country have more than an eight or
\

a ten hour day and some of them get very little for their services.
I am going to use this by way of illustration, although it may lend strength to the argument advanced by the hon. member for West Peterboro. Personally, I may say that I have always been a strong believer in competition. I believe that it is as essential to proper development as anything could possibly be. But unfortunately there is a tendency on the part of this country and many other countries do enact legislation to keep people all their life in a sort of straight jacket or in the nursery, so to speak. There is too much of a tendency to legislate people into doing things whether they really feel disposed to do them or not. I have always believed that when boys and girls reach adolescence they become endowed with sufficient intelligence to be thrown on their own resources. One of the first things that a child meets with when it enters the school is competition, and I believe competition is vitally necessary to the proper development of the child. The fact that children are in competition with one another during the course of their education develops faculties which enable them as they grow up to make the best of their opportunities in life. Now we propose legislation that will make such competition unnecessary.
Legislation has been passed by many bodies of organized labour restricting the amount of work that a man shall do, so that he is held in check. Now, according to this resolution, it is proposed to say to him: You must work only so many hours a day. Work is what is required in the world to-day, and it does not matter how much we may be favourable to an eight-hour day, I believe it is absolutely essential that we should defer taking any action in the matter until we get on our feet again and have overcome some of the difficulties now facing us, the natural result of sacrifices due to the war.
The late James J. Hill, the sage of the West, some years ago stated that inside twenty years the world would be up against starvation. To-day the situation is a very serious and critical one indeed. It is somewhat significant that almost all those who have spoken on this resolution are not employers of labour to any great extent. I believe that the large employers and their employees are arriving at a satisfactory solution of their difficulties, and that Parliament is not called upon at the present
time to enact legislation to make it compulsory for people to do what they ought to do by mutual consent.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of discussing this matter at length, but I want again to reiterate that these restrictions on outppt are bound to affect industries that may not be organized and have taken no steps to protect themselves. I believe the very fact that you make conditions so much more desirable in certain walks of life has a tendency to attract people to them, until eventually you have an over-supply, with the result that some other industry essential to the welfare of the community suffers. I am convinced that that is what is the matter with the world to-day so far as food production is concerned. It was the case in most of the countries in Europe prior to the war, it is the case in the United States to-day, as it is also the case in Canada. This condition has not come about quickly; it has been a gradual growth extending over many years, until it has eventually _ brought about the very thing that organized labour sought to obtain for itself, that is, the elimination of competition. Production has become so curtailed and supplies consequently have become so scarce that prices of food are abnormally high, unorganized industry is reaping advantages that it would not have secured had there been a great many more people in that class. That is the way it is affecting agriculture at the present time.' As I have said, I am not too sure that those who engage in agriculture would suffer as the result of the establishment of an eight-hour day. But I do want to utter a word of warning against the danger which will threaten the lives of millions during the coming year if we curtail and restrict the production of food, which an eight-hour day will undoubtedly do. Weather conditions are variable and uncertain, and in view of the extent to which people are deserting agricultural occupations all over the world I think it would be foolhardy on our part to consider such legislation as is suggested by this resolution under present conditions.
On motion of Mr. I. E. Argue (Swift Current) the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 10.20 p.m:



Friday, March 12, 1920.
